chapter.name: The World of Metals and Non-metals
chapter.blurb: Properties of metals and non-metals, rusting and corrosion, reactions in air and water, and the uses of non-metals and alloys.

scope_in.item: Reactions with air and water and oxides

concepts.name: Lustre, hardness and malleability of metals
concepts.description: Metallic lustre, hardness, malleability and brittleness, with examples such as sodium and mercury and the role of iron in Indian civilisation.
concepts.idea: Metals are generally lustrous, hard and malleable, while non-metals such as coal and sulfur are brittle.
concepts.rule: Ironsmiths heat iron in coal furnaces and beat it with a hammer to shape tools like axes, tawas and spades. Copper, aluminium and iron are lustrous and hard; the shine of metals is called metallic lustre. Coal, sulfur and wood are non-lustrous and not as hard. Some metals such as sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife and mercury is liquid at room temperature. The property by which materials can be beaten into thin sheets is malleability; gold and silver are the most malleable, and silver foil on sweets and aluminium foil come from this. Coal and sulfur break into pieces and are brittle; wood is neither malleable nor brittle. Harappans used copper and gold but hardly iron; once iron became common its strength made ploughs superior.
concepts.example: Aluminium foil for wrapping food is possible because aluminium is malleable.

concepts.name: Ductility and sonority
concepts.description: Drawing metals into wires, uses of wires and steel ropes, and the ringing sound of metals.
concepts.idea: Metals can be drawn into wires and produce a ringing sound.
concepts.rule: The property by which materials can be drawn into wires is ductility, mainly possessed by metals. Copper and aluminium wires are used in electrical fittings; ornaments and stringed instruments such as veena, sitar, violin and guitar use metal wires. Gold is so ductile that one gram can be drawn into a wire 2 km long. Coal and sulfur are not ductile. Steel, a mixture of iron and carbon, makes ropes that support heavy loads in suspension bridges and cranes. Metals that produce a ringing sound when struck are sonorous; a spoon, plate or coin dropped gives a ringing sound while coal and wood give a dull sound. School bells and ghungroos ring because of sonority.
concepts.example: One gram of gold can be drawn into a 2 km long wire.

concepts.name: Conduction of heat and electricity by metals
concepts.description: Metals as good conductors of heat and electricity, and why handles and gloves are made of insulating materials.
concepts.idea: Metals conduct heat and electricity well, so cooking vessels and wires are metal while handles and coverings are insulating.
concepts.rule: When a metal spoon and a wooden spoon are placed in hot water, the metal spoon becomes hotter to touch because heat transfers through it; wood is a poor conductor of heat. The transfer of heat from one point to another in a material is conduction. Metals are good conductors of heat, so cooking vessels are metal with handles of wood or other materials that do not conduct heat. Using a tester circuit, aluminium, iron and copper make the bulb glow while sulfur, coal, wood, stone, rubber eraser and nylon rope do not. Materials that let electricity flow easily are good conductors of electricity; others are poor conductors. Screwdrivers have plastic handles and electricians wear rubber gloves for protection.
concepts.example: The upper end of a metal spoon in hot water becomes hot; the wooden spoon does not.

concepts.name: Rusting and corrosion of iron and other metals
concepts.description: The experiment on rusting, conditions needed for rust, corrosion of other metals and prevention, and the Iron Pillar of Delhi.
concepts.idea: Iron rusts in the presence of both moist air, and corrosion can be prevented by covering the metal.
concepts.rule: Iron objects left open develop a brown deposit called rust; the process is rusting. In the experiment, a nail in bottle A with dry air and silica gel does not rust, a nail in B under boiled water covered with oil does not rust, but a nail in C partly in water and open to air rusts. So both air and water are needed. Silica gel keeps air dry. Other metals also discolour: copper gets a green coating and silver a black one. Gradual damage of metal surfaces by air, water or other substances is corrosion. Rusting costs a great deal every year. Rusting can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing and galvanisation (a zinc coating). The Iron Pillar of Delhi, over 1600 years old, about 8 m high and over 6000 kg, has barely any rust.
concepts.example: Boiled and cooled water removes dissolved gases in the experiment.

concepts.name: Metals and non-metals in air and water: oxides
concepts.description: Burning magnesium, sodium in kerosene, burning sulfur, phosphorus in water, and acidic and basic oxides.
concepts.idea: Metal oxides are generally basic and non-metal oxides are acidic; non-metals like sulfur do not react with water.
concepts.rule: Magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame and forms white magnesium oxide from reaction with oxygen. A solution of the oxide turns red litmus blue, so it is basic; generally oxides of metals are basic. Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and water, releasing much heat, so it is stored in kerosene. Sulfur burnt in a deflagrating spoon forms sulfur dioxide; dissolved in water it forms sulfurous acid, which turns blue litmus red, so it is acidic. Sulfur does not react with water. Phosphorus catches fire in air and is stored in water. Non-metals like sulfur and phosphorus are soft, dull, not malleable, ductile or sonorous and are poor conductors; their oxides are acidic. Metals and non-metals are elements; 118 elements are known.
concepts.example: Sodium is stored in kerosene and phosphorus in water.

concepts.name: Non-metals in daily life, alloys and recycling
concepts.description: Uses of oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, chlorine and iodine, alloys and special metals, and recycling of metals.
concepts.idea: Non-metals are essential for life, and metals and alloys are recycled to save resources.
concepts.rule: Non-metals matter in everyday life. We breathe oxygen to survive. Carbon is the building block of all life forms and a key part of proteins, fats and carbohydrates. Nitrogen is used to make fertilisers and is an essential nutrient for plants. Chlorine is used to purify water and an iodine solution is applied on wounds as an antiseptic. Alloys are mixtures of two or more metals or of a metal and a non-metal, and are important for utensils and tools and in almost every industry. Zirconium is used in atomic energy and titanium in aerospace. In India metals like iron and aluminium are recycled to reduce waste and support sustainability. Metals differ from non-metals in lustre, malleability, ductility and conduction, and their oxides are basic while non-metal oxides are acidic.
concepts.example: Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon.
